signs.title: Zodiac signs and decans
signs.history:
The signs of the Western zodiac developed gradually from the astronomical and astrological traditions of Mesopotamia. The division of the Sun's apparent path into twelve equal parts was later adopted and developed in the Greek world. In the tropical zodiac, the beginning of Aries corresponds to the spring equinox: signs refer to sectors used for measurement, not to the visible boundaries of constellations. The precession of the equinoxes explains why these two divisions no longer coincide.

Decans have a separate and older history. In ancient Egypt, groups of stars, traditionally numbering thirty-six, were used to track the hours of the night. Evidence of them survives in the star clocks depicted on coffins from the Middle Kingdom. Hellenistic astrology subsequently incorporated decans into the zodiac, dividing each thirty-degree sign into three ten-degree sections. Successive traditions assigned different planetary correspondences to them.
signs.principle:
The tropical zodiac divides a 360-degree circle into twelve signs of 30 degrees each. It identifies the section occupied by the Sun at the time of birth. Each sign is traditionally assigned an element, a modality and a ruling planet. These categories form a symbolic vocabulary for describing tendencies and contrasts, rather than a measurement of personality.

A decan provides a finer division: each sign contains three 10-degree sections, making thirty-six decans in all. Astrological schools do not all assign them the same planets. Affinities between signs are also based on conventions, particularly associations between elements. A reading of a sign and decan is therefore primarily an interpretation within a system of correspondences.
signs.zodiac:
ZODIAC uses the tropical zodiac. It determines the sign from the 30-degree section occupied by the Sun at birth, then the decan from the 10-degree section within that sign. There are three decans per sign, or thirty-six in total.

The Sun's position is calculated directly on the device using corrected formulas by Jean Meeus. Comparison with the astropy astronomy library indicates a difference of approximately 0.008 degrees between 1900 and 2100. When the birth time is unknown, ZODIAC uses noon. If the Sun crosses a sign or decan boundary during that day, the result is marked as 'uncertain'.

Each sign is assigned an element, a modality and a ruling planet. In particular, ZODIAC uses Pluto for Scorpio, Uranus for Aquarius and Neptune for Pisces. For decans, it follows the triplicity method: the assigned planet rules a sign of the same element, following zodiacal order. Affinities between signs come from a traditional table based on the elements.
signs.notThis: The Sun's position can be calculated astronomically; that does not mean the human qualities associated with signs and decans have scientific validation. These symbolic portraits do not necessarily describe your experience and do not announce future events. You may find one idea useful, set another aside or choose not to use this reading.
sources: Otto Neugebauer and Richard A. Parker, Egyptian Astronomical Texts, vol. 1: The Early Decans, 1960.
Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos, 2nd century (F. E. Robbins edition, 1940).
Nicholas Campion, A History of Western Astrology, vol. 1: The Ancient World, 2009.
Jean Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, 2nd edition, 1998.

chinese.title: Chinese zodiac
chinese.history:
The Chinese zodiac belongs to a tradition of calendars and cycles that is organised differently from Western zodiac signs. The twelve Earthly Branches and ten Heavenly Stems are used to name years and other units of time. Combining them produces a sequence of sixty stages, often called the sexagenary cycle. The twelve animals associated with the branches are documented by the Han dynasty at the latest, but their precise origins remain a subject of historical debate.

Over time, the animals, five elements and alternation of yin and yang formed a set of correspondences widely passed down in China and several other parts of Asia. The traditional Chinese calendar is lunisolar: it coordinates months linked to lunar cycles with the solar year. Practices are not entirely uniform. Some astrological schools use the beginning of spring, around 4 February, to mark the change of symbolic year, whereas popular customs often follow Lunar New Year.
chinese.principle:
In its best-known annual form, the Chinese zodiac associates each year with one of twelve animals: Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Goat, Monkey, Rooster, Dog and Pig. The cycle is not limited to these animals, however. The ten Heavenly Stems introduce the five elements, each associated with a yin or yang polarity. Together, the branches and stems form a sixty-year sequence.

An hour can also be assigned an animal, as the day is divided into twelve two-hour periods. Traditional relationships between animals describe connections, tensions or positions without any particular classification. These are cultural and symbolic categories: they offer a language for comparison, not a verifiable description of a person.
chinese.zodiac:
ZODIAC assigns the year's animal from the Earthly Branch and the element and yin or yang polarity from the Heavenly Stem. To determine which year applies, it follows Lunar New Year, using a built-in table covering 1900 to 2101, cross-checked against new moon calculations. Thus, a birth on 26 January 1990 still belongs to the Year of the Snake, not the Year of the Horse.

If a birth time is provided, ZODIAC adds the animal corresponding to its two-hour period. For example, the Rat covers 23:00 to 00:59. For relationships between animals, the application uses the six harmonies, trines, the opposition known as a 'clash', harm, punishment, self-punishment and neutral relationships.

There are several conventions for changing years. Some traditions use a point around 4 February. ZODIAC does not mix these conventions: it explicitly uses Lunar New Year for the reading it provides.
chinese.notThis: These associations do not establish anyone's individual character or the quality of a relationship. They are not a scientific assessment and do not determine which choices to make. Any value they offer is cultural, narrative or personal. You are free to regard them as a symbolic heritage, compare different conventions or attach no personal significance to them.
sources: Edward M. Reingold and Nachum Dershowitz, Calendrical Calculations: The Ultimate Edition, 2018.
Derek Walters, Ming Shu: The Art and Practice of Chinese Astrology, 1987.
Nicholas Campion, Astrology and Cosmology in the World's Religions, 2012.

natal.title: Birth chart
natal.history:
The birth chart is part of the history of horoscopic astrology, developed in antiquity from Mesopotamian knowledge and Greek innovations. It represents celestial positions for a particular time and place of birth. In the Hellenistic world, writers organised signs, planets, angles, houses and angular relationships between celestial bodies into a language of interpretation. In the 2nd century, Ptolemy set out several of these principles in the Tetrabiblos.

Techniques continued to develop during the Middle Ages, notably through works transmitted in Arabic, and later in Renaissance Europe. There is no single way of dividing houses. The system known as Placidus is associated with Placido de Titis, a 17th-century Italian astrologer. Modern astronomy subsequently made it possible to calculate celestial positions far more accurately than with ancient tables, without thereby validating their astrological interpretation.
natal.principle:
A birth chart shows the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets at a chosen moment. Signs indicate sectors of the zodiac, while houses symbolically organise different areas of experience according to the orientation of the sky at the relevant location and time. The ascendant and Midheaven are geometric reference points linked to that orientation.

Aspects compare the angular separations between celestial bodies. A conjunction brings two positions together, while an opposition separates them by half a circle; the sextile, square and trine correspond to other angles emphasised by tradition. An orb allows a margin around each angle. Houses, orbs and assigned meanings may vary between schools. The chart remains an interpretative construction based on astronomical data.
natal.zodiac:
ZODIAC calculates the positions of the Sun, Moon and eight planets on the device. Planetary calculations are based on JPL orbits established by E. M. Standish, with corrections; the positions of the Moon and Sun use Jean Meeus's methods. Between 1900 and 2100, measured differences against astropy range from approximately 0.008 degrees for the Sun to around 0.06 degrees for Uranus.

The local birth time is converted to Universal Time using the city's official time zone, taking historical daylight-saving changes into account. The integrated GeoNames database contains 33,955 cities. When the time and place are known, the application calculates the ascendant, Midheaven and Placidus houses. Otherwise, it shows neither an ascendant nor houses.

The aspects included are conjunction and opposition with an 8-degree orb, square and trine with 7 degrees, and sextile with 5 degrees. Here, retrograde motion means a decreasing longitude.
natal.notThis: The accuracy of astronomical coordinates does not prove any connection between a celestial configuration and your personality. A chart is neither a scientific measure of your life nor a statement about future events. Houses and aspects are interpreted according to traditions that allow several variants. You may read this diagram as a symbolic representation without handing over your decisions to it.
sources: Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos, 2nd century (F. E. Robbins edition, 1940).
Placido de Titis, Tabulae Primi Mobilis, 1657.
Robert Hand, Horoscope Symbols, 1981.
Jean Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, 2nd edition, 1998.
E. M. Standish, Keplerian Elements for Approximate Positions of the Major Planets, Jet Propulsion Laboratory (NASA) document.

sky.title: Sky right now
sky.history:
Observing the movements of the Sun, Moon and planets is an activity far older than present-day astrology. Civilisations developed calendars, tracked eclipses and identified stars to measure time and mark the seasons. In Mediterranean antiquity, astronomers developed geometric methods for describing the apparent movements of celestial bodies. These observations also contributed to traditions of astrological interpretation.

The idea of comparing the sky at a particular moment with a birth chart belongs to this history of transits. It has taken many forms and remains part of contemporary horoscopes. Meanwhile, mapping the sky has evolved through star catalogues, observing instruments and astronomical calculations. The constellations used today as reference areas must not be confused with tropical signs. ZODIAC brings together two distinct approaches: showing calculable celestial phenomena and offering a symbolic reading of certain planetary positions.
sky.principle:
A view of the current sky shows the present arrangement of celestial bodies. In an astrological reading, a transit compares a current position with a natal reference point: the proximity or separation between zodiac sectors is given a traditional meaning. Apparent movements in the opposite direction, called retrograde motion, and the phases of the Moon are also commonly discussed reference points.

An observable sky map answers a different question: which celestial bodies are in which directions from a given location? Its representation depends on the observation point and time. Eclipses and lunar phases are astronomical phenomena, whereas comments about transits are interpretations. Distinguishing these two levels helps you read the whole without confusing them.
sky.zodiac:
ZODIAC produces a daily or weekly horoscope from calculated planetary positions. For its 'whole-sign' reading, it compares the sign of a current planet with that of the natal Sun: the same sign, trine, square or opposition. The texts distinguish broader trends, from Jupiter to Pluto, from the current atmosphere, from the Sun to Mars. The application also presents retrograde motions and lunar phases. When the birth time and place are known, it adds transits to the birth chart.

The sky map visible from a location includes 921 stars, 88 constellations and planets visible to the naked eye, using a projection centred on the zenith. ZODIAC also displays solar eclipses visible from that location, with estimated times accurate to approximately 35 seconds, and a calendar covering the next 30 days. These calculations take place on the device, without a connection. Astronomical data and symbolic commentary on them remain two different things.
sky.notThis: The positions of celestial bodies, lunar phases and eclipses are astronomical data; the interpretation of a transit is not a scientific conclusion about what will happen in your life. A daily horoscope is no substitute for observing the sky or exercising your own judgement. You may use the map to discover the sky while setting symbolic readings aside.
sources: James Evans, The History and Practice of Ancient Astronomy, 1998.
Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos, 2nd century (F. E. Robbins edition, 1940).
Jean Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, 2nd edition, 1998.
Fred Espenak and Jean Meeus, Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000, 2006.

compat.title: Symbolic compatibility
compat.history:
Comparing astrological charts is a practice rooted in traditions of relationship astrology. In antiquity, some writers, including Ptolemy, discussed unions and partnerships in their astrological works. Methods of comparison subsequently changed across periods, schools and uses. Modern synastry, in particular, places the positions of two charts side by side to seek symbolic connections and contrasts.

Other traditions offer their own systems of correspondences. The Chinese zodiac associates years with animals and cycles, while modern Western numerology assigns meanings to numbers calculated from birth dates. Bringing these together in a single overview is a contemporary choice, not one unified method handed down unchanged from antiquity. These frameworks have different histories. Placing them side by side may encourage discussion of expectations and differences, but it does not provide a way to measure human relationships.
compat.principle:
An astrological comparison by sign examines whether positions fall in sectors traditionally considered close, complementary or contrasting. Synastry by degree adds a finer reading of the angles between two charts. Numerology groups certain numbers into symbolic families. The Chinese zodiac uses annual categories distinct from the Western zodiac.

These approaches share neither the same origins nor the same units of calculation. Combining them therefore requires explicit conventions and attention to uncertainties. An area of contrast does not mean a relationship will fail; an area of harmony does not mean it will work. Real behaviour, communication and choices cannot be reduced to a table of correspondences.
compat.zodiac:
ZODIAC examines nine areas: emotions through the Moons, affection through Venus, attraction by comparing one person's Venus with the other's Mars in both directions, communication through Mercury, temperaments through the Suns, drive and disagreements through Mars, first impressions through ascendants when birth times and places are known, Life paths through the number families 1-5-7, 2-4-8 and 3-6-9, and finally the Chinese zodiac.

For planets, the separation between signs ranges from 0 to 6. Separations of 0, 2 and 4 indicate harmony; 6 indicates complementarity; and 1, 3 and 5 indicate an area requiring attention. No overall score is given: ZODIAC presents a summary of harmonies, complementarities, areas requiring attention and areas analysed, together with an overview and advice.

When the time is unknown and a planet changes sign during the day, both possibilities are tested. If the interpretation changes, the area is marked 'uncertain' and excluded from the summary. Detailed synastry, using degrees and orbs of 4 to 6 degrees, complements this sign-based reading and can sometimes give a different interpretation.
compat.notThis: This overview assesses neither a person's worth nor the actual strength of a relationship. No astrological or numerological method can establish individual compatibility scientifically. Differences classified as favourable or difficult are conventions, not verdicts. It is better to consider what the people involved say, do and want rather than rely on a comparison of symbols.
sources: Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos, 2nd century (F. E. Robbins edition, 1940).
Robert Hand, Horoscope Symbols, 1981.
Nicholas Campion, A History of Western Astrology, vol. 2: The Medieval and Modern Worlds, 2009.
Faith Javane and Dusty Bunker, Numerology and the Divine Triangle, 1979.

numerology.title: Numerology
numerology.history:
Associating numbers with ideas, letters or qualities occurs in several ancient cultures. Greek traditions developed philosophical reflections on numbers, while other systems assigned numerical values to letters. This does not mean contemporary Western numerology was established by Pythagoras: that connection is a traditional attribution, not a demonstrated historical fact.

The modern practice of reducing letters to values from 1 to 9 and interpreting numbers derived from birth dates and names became particularly widespread in the United States in the early 20th century. The writings of L. Dow Balliett are among the documented milestones of this spread. Other works subsequently developed various categories and interpretations. Conventions differ between authors, particularly over which numbers to retain, ambiguous letters and how names are written. Present-day numerology is therefore a family of methods rather than a single ancient rule.
numerology.principle:
Numerology converts written information, such as a date or name, into numbers. It adds digits according to chosen rules, then assigns a symbolic meaning to the result. The Life path uses the birth date; name numbers use letters. Personal cycles apply the same logic to shorter periods.

Reduction generally brings results down to smaller numbers. Some schools nevertheless retain 11, 22 and 33, known as 'master numbers'. The way alphabets and vowels are handled also has consequences. Two methods may therefore produce different results, neither of which is an objective measurement of personality. The meaning assigned to a result depends on the system of interpretation adopted.
numerology.zodiac:
For the Life path, ZODIAC reduces the day, month and year of birth separately, adds the three results, then reduces the total. It retains the master numbers 11, 22 and 33. Name numbers include expression, calculated from all letters; the inner number, from vowels; and personality, from consonants.

For names written in the Latin alphabet, letters receive the values known as Pythagorean: A is 1, through to I at 9, then the sequence restarts with J at 1. Accents are ignored. Y counts as a vowel when it is not next to another vowel. ZODIAC uses an abjad for Arabic and a Cyrillic table for Russian. For other writing systems, the application asks you to enter the name in Latin letters.

ZODIAC also calculates personal cycles: the year within a nine-year sequence, the month and the day. These are numerical conventions applied consistently, not measurements of personal traits.
numerology.notThis: There is no scientific validation for using these associations to infer your character or future from a name or date. A variation in spelling, alphabet or rule may change the result. You can use these numbers as prompts for reflection, but they have no authority over your identity or decisions.
sources: L. Dow Balliett, The Philosophy of Numbers ; Their Tone and Colors, 1908.
Faith Javane and Dusty Bunker, Numerology and the Divine Triangle, 1979.
Nicholas Campion, A History of Western Astrology, vol. 2: The Medieval and Modern Worlds, 2009.

square.title: Pythagoras Square
square.history:
The name 'Pythagoras Square' draws on the symbolic authority often attributed to numbers in the Pythagorean tradition. It may suggest that a personality grid based on the birth date came directly from the Greek philosopher. There is no evidence establishing such historical continuity. The square known as the 'psychomatrix' belongs to much more recent numerology.

This method is associated with Alexander F. Alexandrov, a Russian author who developed a system for the numerical analysis of dates in the late 20th century. He describes a grid in which digits and their repetitions are given symbolic meanings. Later publications and contemporary calculators spread variants of this approach. Some rules used today, particularly for years beginning with 20, do not necessarily match Alexandrov's original procedure. Distinguishing the traditional name, the modern author and recent adaptations avoids attributing a present-day method to antiquity.
square.principle:
The square is a grid of three rows and three columns containing the digits 1 to 9. The digits in a date of birth and in auxiliary numbers called 'working numbers' are recorded. Repetitions are interpreted as symbolic intensities; an empty cell may receive a different reading from one containing many digits.

The eight lines of interpretation bring together several cells and suggest other connections. Because dates do not contain the same digits in every century, the system can produce different distributions across generations. The grid is therefore not a psychological measurement. Its results depend on the rules chosen, particularly the treatment of working numbers and the year of birth.
square.zodiac:
ZODIAC constructs a 3 × 3 grid from the digits of the birth date and four working numbers. The first is the sum of all the digits in the date; the second is the sum of the digits of the first. For a birth before 2000, the third is the first minus twice the first non-zero digit of the day, following Alexandrov's method. From 2000 onwards, ZODIAC instead uses the first plus 19, a modern variant found in current calculators; Alexandrov retained subtraction. The fourth is the sum of the digits of the third.

Zeros are not counted in the cells. The grid has nine cells, corresponding to the digits 1 to 9, and eight lines of interpretation. ZODIAC distinguishes three levels for these lines: subtle, balanced and pronounced. Their calibration is separate for births before 2000 and from 2000 onwards because the digits found in dates are not distributed in the same way. An empty cell is presented as a quality to cultivate.
square.notThis: The psychomatrix does not measure scientifically recognised abilities or personality traits. The change of formula from 2000 onwards also shows that the result depends on editorial conventions. An empty cell is neither an established deficiency nor a judgement about you. You may use this diagram as an invitation to reflect without giving it any power of assessment.
sources: Alexander F. Alexandrov, Прогнозирование жизненных событий с помощью чисел (Predicting Life Events Using Numbers), 2015.

portrait.title: Symbolic portrait
portrait.history:
The symbolic portrait brings together several traditions that developed in different periods. The Western zodiac and its decans originated in ancient developments, while numerology based on names and dates, in its common Western form, spread widely in the modern period. Tarot cards appeared in 15th-century Italy as playing cards. Their esoteric interpretation developed much later, mainly from the late 18th century onwards.

In London, the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, founded in 1888, systematised correspondences between signs, planets and cards. These associations influenced 20th-century tarot readings, particularly around the Waite-Smith deck published in 1909. ZODIAC's portrait therefore does not reproduce a single ancient tradition. It combines systems with different origins, making its chosen correspondences and the differences in numbering between decks explicit.
portrait.principle:
The portrait links numbers derived from birth to the major arcana of the tarot, then connects astrological reference points to other cards. Each card offers images and themes for a symbolic reading. These correspondences are not based on a physical relationship between numbers, planets and illustrations; they belong to a language passed down by certain schools.

The purpose of this combination is to present several perspectives on the same set of birth data. Arcana obtained through numerical calculations do not play the same role as cards associated with signs, planets or decans. The choice of deck also matters: Strength and Justice do not have the same numbers everywhere. A coherent reading must therefore state its conventions.
portrait.zodiac:
ZODIAC connects numerology, tarot and the zodiac. It presents two major arcana calculated from birth information. The birth card comes from adding the day, month and year, then reducing the sum until the number is no greater than 22. The Life path arcana follow a different correspondence: numbers 1 to 9 give the arcana with the same number; 11 gives arcana XI; 22 corresponds to the Fool; and 33 corresponds to arcana VI.

The application also uses the correspondences of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. It associates one major arcana card with the zodiac sign, another with the ruling planet and a minor arcana card with the decan. These are traditional correspondences, not astronomical calculations.

Finally, ZODIAC respects the numbering of the selected deck. Arcana VIII and XI, assigned to Strength and Justice, are reversed between the Marseille tarot and the Waite-Smith deck. The labels therefore follow the chosen deck.
portrait.notThis: No calculation in the portrait establishes an individual trait, a vocation or a future event. Cards and numbers form interpretative associations whose meanings may change between traditions and decks. You may appreciate their images, question a connection or keep none of them. The portrait remains a suggested reading with no scientific authority over your life.
sources: Michael Dummett, The Game of Tarot: From Ferrara to Salt Lake City, 1980.
Ronald Decker, Thierry Depaulis and Michael Dummett, A Wicked Pack of Cards: The Origins of the Occult Tarot, 1996.
Israel Regardie, The Golden Dawn, 1937-1940.
Arthur Edward Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, 1910.

tarot.title: Tarot and spreads
tarot.history:
Playing cards spread through Europe in the late 14th century. In the 15th century, decks with trump cards called 'trionfi' appeared in Italy; they are the origin of tarot decks. Their first documented use was for playing games, not for symbolic consultation. The model often called the 'Tarot de Marseille' took shape gradually during the 17th and 18th centuries through families of printed decks.

Divinatory interpretations of tarot emerged in the late 18th century, notably with the writings of Antoine Court de Gébelin in 1781 and the practices of Etteilla. These authors proposed origins and meanings that must not be confused with established historical facts. In 1909, Pamela Colman Smith illustrated the deck developed with Arthur Edward Waite, giving the numbered cards distinctive pictorial scenes. Contemporary uses range from card games to personal reflection, with various methods of laying out the cards.
tarot.principle:
A complete tarot deck contains 78 cards, including 22 major arcana and 56 minor arcana. The images evoke themes, situations or symbolic tensions. In a spread, a card's position gives it a function: describing a situation, raising a question or suggesting a line of reflection. Several cards can be read together as parts of a narrative.

Chance determines which cards are selected, but it does not establish a causal relationship with the question asked. Some practices consider reversed cards and assign them an additional nuance. Others ignore them. No spread imposes a single interpretation: the meaning depends on the deck, each card's position and the way you read the images.
tarot.zodiac:
ZODIAC offers two decks, Marseille and Waite-Smith, with original illustrations generated using Google's Gemini and OpenAI's ChatGPT. You can use the 22 major arcana or the complete 78-card deck. Reversed cards are optional.

The application presents a birth card, calculated by adding the day, month and year, then reducing the result to no more than 22. It also offers a card of the day: for the same person, it remains unchanged throughout the day. It is derived from a digital fingerprint combining their date of birth and the current date, and is selected from the 22 major arcana.

Four types of spread are available: 'One question · One card', 'Past · Present · Future', 'Situation · Challenge · Advice' and 'The next six months'. Shuffling uses the browser's cryptographic randomness and the Fisher-Yates algorithm: choosing a face-down card therefore draws it at random. The limit is one spread per day per type, or one per month for the six-month spread. The question stays on the device.
tarot.notThis: A spread does not establish what will happen and cannot serve as evidence of another person's intentions. Even when selection is random, interpretation remains subjective. You may use it to formulate a question or consider different angles, but no card makes decisions for you. You remain free not to follow the advice offered.
sources: Michael Dummett, The Game of Tarot: From Ferrara to Salt Lake City, 1980.
Ronald Decker, Thierry Depaulis and Michael Dummett, A Wicked Pack of Cards: The Origins of the Occult Tarot, 1996.
Arthur Edward Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, 1910.

oracle.title: Yes / No Oracle
oracle.history: Answers selected by drawing lots appear in many ancient and modern practices. Games based on closed questions, with a limited set of outcomes, are a simple example. ZODIAC's Yes / No Oracle does not claim to reproduce any particular historical ritual. It simply takes the general idea of letting chance select an answer from several possibilities.
oracle.principle: A question receives a randomly chosen answer. The mechanism does not try to understand what the question means: it selects an option from a fixed set. The answer may provide a starting point for reflection, but contains no verified information about the situation concerning you.
oracle.zodiac: ZODIAC offers four answers: 'Yes', 'No', 'Maybe' and 'Soon'. Each has exactly a one-in-four chance of being selected. The draw uses the browser's cryptographic randomness. The interface arrow stops on the answer already selected. Nothing is written down or saved. There is no calculation here involving your birth, the sky or a deck of cards: this is a random draw independent of your question.
oracle.notThis: The oracle knows neither your situation nor what will happen. An equal chance for each answer does not make any of them more accurate. This game is not a scientific decision-making tool. You may use it for entertainment or as a prompt for reflection, without letting it make your choices.
